questions.question: The main purpose of the passage is to:
questions.solution: Paragraph 1 describes mangroves, paragraph 2 their benefits, and paragraph 3 why they are lost and how restoration can work. The passage never promotes fish farms (they are a cause of clearing), never mentions replacing towns, and never compares mangroves with rainforests.
options: explain what mangroves are, why they are valuable and why protecting them is difficult
encourage the building of fish farms along tropical coasts
argue that mangroves should replace coastal towns

questions.question: According to the passage, pneumatophores help mangroves to:
questions.solution: 'These breathing roots, called pneumatophores, take in air at low tide', because 'the mud holds very little oxygen'. Salt filtering, trapping sediment and storing carbon are described separately and not linked to pneumatophores.
options: take in air, because the mud holds very little oxygen

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as a benefit of mangroves?
questions.solution: Erosion protection, the nursery role and carbon storage are all in paragraph 2. Timber for shipbuilding is never mentioned; the only wood use given is firewood for local communities.
options: Sheltering young fish, crabs and prawns

questions.question: According to the passage, newly planted mangroves are often lost again when:
questions.solution: The last sentence says 'Without such involvement' (of local communities), newly planted areas are often lost again. Sheltered mud and the fresh/salt mix are conditions seedlings need, not causes of loss.
options: local communities are not involved in planting and protecting them
seedlings are planted in sheltered mud
the water has a mix of fresh and salt water

questions.question: Why had the radio not been used for eleven years?
questions.solution: The grandfather says: 'Nothing in it has worked since your grandmother passed away.' The valves were still inside, and nothing suggests he disliked the news or lent it out.
options: It had stopped working around the time Meera's grandmother died
Meera's grandfather disliked listening to the news
It had been lent to Meera's uncle
Its glass valves had been removed

questions.question: The detail that the grandfather 'had not turned a page in an hour' suggests that he:
questions.solution: He 'pretended to read the newspaper', so his attention was really on Meera and the radio. Nothing in the story suggests anger, eyesight problems or sleep.
options: was quietly watching Meera's work with interest
was angry with Meera for opening the radio
was reading slowly because of poor eyesight
had fallen asleep in his chair

questions.question: What had Meera learned from her summer at the repair shop?
questions.solution: The passage states this directly: 'she had learned that most broken things were not as broken as people believed'.
options: That most broken things are not as broken as people believe
That old radios cannot be repaired
That soldering is too dangerous for beginners
That valves are more reliable than wires

questions.question: The last line, 'she had repaired more than a radio', most likely means that:
questions.solution: The radio had been silent since the grandmother's death, and the grandfather tunes it to a song 'She liked'. The 'more' that was repaired is emotional. The dial is never fixed, and nothing is said about a shop or the radio's future.
options: fixing the radio also brought back, for her grandfather, a connection to his late wife
she had also fixed the cracked dial
she would now open a repair shop of her own
the radio would never break again

questions.question: 'The air thick enough to lean on' is an example of:
questions.solution: It is a deliberate exaggeration (air cannot really be leaned on) used to convey heavy humidity, which is hyperbole. It does not use 'like' or 'as' (simile), imitate a sound (onomatopoeia) or repeat initial consonants (alliteration).

questions.question: 'Leaves turn their pale undersides to the sky, as if to check what is coming' is an example of:
questions.solution: The leaves are given a human intention ('to check what is coming'), which is personification.

questions.question: The shopkeepers 'complain instead about the mud, though their faces say otherwise'. This suggests that they:
questions.solution: Their words complain, but 'their faces say otherwise', meaning their expressions show pleasure. The other options take the complaint at face value or add details that aren't there.
options: are secretly glad that the rain has come
are angrier about the mud than they were about the heat
want the hot weather to return
are about to close their shops

questions.question: As used in the last line, the word 'reprieve' most nearly means:
questions.solution: After days of oppressive heat, the rain is 'not weather' but relief, a temporary escape from something unpleasant. That is the meaning of reprieve.
options: a welcome relief from something unpleasant

questions.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to DILIGENT.
questions.solution: Diligent means showing steady, careful effort, i.e. hard-working. Intelligent is a different quality, and careless is the opposite.

questions.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to CANDID.
questions.solution: Candid means honest and direct, i.e. frank. Secretive and cunning are nearly opposite, and polite is unrelated.

questions.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to ABUNDANT.
questions.solution: Abundant means existing in large quantities, i.e. plentiful. Scarce is its antonym.

questions.question: Choose the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to TRANSPARENT.
questions.solution: Transparent means that light passes through; opaque means that it does not. Clear is a synonym.

questions.question: Choose the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to EXPAND.
questions.solution: To expand is to become larger; to contract is to become smaller. Enlarge and extend are synonyms.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: The committee has not yet ______ a decision on the proposal.
questions.solution: 'Reach a decision' is the standard collocation. 'Arrived' would need 'at'; 'done a decision' and 'made up a decision' are not idiomatic.

questions.question: Fill in the blanks: She is good ______ mathematics but weak ______ spelling.
questions.solution: The idioms are 'good at' a subject and 'weak in' a subject. Only the first pair puts 'at' after 'good'.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: Neither the manager nor his assistants ______ present at the meeting.
questions.solution: With 'neither … nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, here the plural 'assistants', and the past tense fits 'at the meeting'. So 'were'.

questions.question: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) Each of the students / (B) have submitted / (C) the project / (D) before the deadline.
questions.solution: 'Each' is singular, so the verb must be 'has submitted'. The error is in part B.

questions.question: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) He has been living / (B) in Pune / (C) since five years / (D) and likes it there.
questions.solution: 'Since' is used with a point in time (since 2020); a period of time takes 'for'. It should be 'for five years'. The error is in part C.

questions.question: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) If I would have known / (B) about the traffic, / (C) I would have left / (D) home earlier.
questions.solution: In a third conditional, the if-clause takes the past perfect: 'If I had known…'. 'Would have' belongs only in the main clause (part C, which is correct). The error is in part A.

questions.question:
Rearrange the parts to form a meaningful sentence:
P: to the station   Q: I ran all the way   R: but still missed   S: the last bus home
questions.solution: 'I ran all the way (Q) to the station (P) but still missed (R) the last bus home (S).' QRSP gives 'the last bus home to the station', which contradicts itself (home or the station?). PRQS breaks 'missed … the last bus' apart, and RSQP begins with 'but' and leaves 'to the station' hanging.

questions.question:
The sentence begins: 'The children…'. Rearrange the parts to complete it:
P: that they fell asleep   Q: were so tired   R: on the sofa   S: before dinner was served
questions.solution: 'The children were so tired (Q) that they fell asleep (P) on the sofa (R) before dinner was served (S).' The 'so … that' pattern needs Q before P. Each other option puts 'that they fell asleep' before 'were so tired', which is ungrammatical.

questions.question:
Rearrange the parts to form a meaningful sentence:
P: the book   Q: that you lent me   R: is   S: very interesting
questions.solution: 'The book (P) that you lent me (Q) is (R) very interesting (S).' The relative clause Q must come right after the noun it describes, 'the book', and then the verb 'is' and its complement follow. PRQS, QRPS and RQSP all separate the clause from its noun or misplace the verb, giving ungrammatical strings.

questions.question:
Match each word in List I with its meaning in List II.
List I: (a) Benevolent (b) Meticulous (c) Ephemeral (d) Gregarious
List II: (i) lasting a very short time (ii) fond of the company of others (iii) kind and generous (iv) very careful about detail
questions.solution: Benevolent = kind and generous (iii); meticulous = very careful about detail (iv); ephemeral = lasting a very short time (i); gregarious = fond of company (ii).

questions.question: The passage is mainly about:
questions.solution: The passage explains what stepwells were, why they were decorated, why they were abandoned and how some are being restored.
options: stepwells: their purpose, beauty, decline and revival
how piped water systems are built in cities
the history of trade routes in western India

questions.question: According to the passage, many stepwells were richly decorated because:
questions.solution: The second paragraph says they were decorated 'because the people who paid for them saw the gift of water as an act of merit'.
options: the people who paid for them saw giving water as an act of merit
kings wanted to attract foreign traders
the carvings kept the water cool
villagers used the sculptures to measure the water level

questions.question: What led to the decline of stepwells?
questions.solution: The third paragraph says the decline began when piped water and hand pumps arrived and water could be drawn without climbing down.
options: The arrival of piped water and hand pumps
A shortage of stone for repairs

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage?
questions.solution: Resting places, silt-clearing by volunteers and the World Heritage status of Rani ki Vav are all stated. Irrigation of large farms is never mentioned.
options: Stepwells were used to irrigate large farms
Stepwells gave travellers a cool place to rest
Some stepwells have been cleared of silt by volunteers
Rani ki Vav is a World Heritage site

questions.question: The restoration work described in the last paragraph suggests that:
questions.solution: The volunteers' view is that structures that store rain where it falls 'may be useful again in regions where groundwater is running low'. The passage does not say they should replace modern supplies.
options: old structures that store rainwater could help regions where groundwater is falling
stepwells should replace all modern water supply
stepwells can only be useful as tourist sites

questions.question: According to the passage, during sleep the brain appears to:
questions.solution: The first paragraph says the brain 'appears to replay and strengthen what was learned', helping to move it into long-term memory.
options: replay and strengthen what was learned during the day
work faster than during the day

questions.question: Why do many teenagers find early school starts difficult?
questions.solution: The third paragraph explains that in adolescence the internal clock shifts later, yet school often starts early in the morning.
options: Their body clock shifts later, so they feel sleepy late at night
They have more homework than younger children
They dislike waking up to alarms
Their schools are far from home

questions.question: The author's attitude to the evidence on later school start times is best described as:
questions.solution: The author reports better attendance and alertness but adds that 'results vary' and 'more studies are needed', which is a cautious view.

questions.question: The statement that sleep is 'part of studying, not a break from it' means that:
questions.solution: The writer argues that sleep helps memory and attention, so it supports study rather than interrupting it.
options: sleep contributes to learning instead of wasting study time
students should never study at night
studying is more tiring than sleeping
a break from studying is the same as sleeping

questions.question: With which statement would the author most likely agree?
questions.solution: The fourth paragraph accepts an occasional late night, while the second paragraph says the effects of short sleep add up when it becomes a habit. The other options contradict the passage.
options: An occasional late night may be unavoidable, but regular short sleep can harm learning
Students should avoid studying after sunset
Sleep has no effect on attention
Later school start times always improve results

questions.question: Why did Arjun hold his bag in front of him 'as if it were a shield'?
questions.solution: A shield protects. The image shows that Arjun felt unsafe and guarded on his first day in a new school.
options: He felt nervous and defensive in a new place
He was angry with his teacher

questions.question: Why did Arjun stay in the classroom at the break?
questions.solution: The passage says he 'had decided, quite firmly, that it was easier not to try'.
options: He had decided it was easier not to try to make friends
He had a test to prepare for
The teacher asked him to stay

questions.question: Imran 'laughed, as though it were a joke against himself'. This suggests that he:
questions.solution: He jokes that nobody comes to the back bench, including himself. The joke is on him, not on Arjun, which shows warmth.
options: is friendly and makes light of his own loneliness at the back
is proud of the last bench

questions.question: What does Imran imply by saying that the work is hard 'only if you're alone'?
questions.solution: He offers his notes and help straight after saying it, which shows that he means help from others makes the work manageable.
options: Difficulties become easier when people help each other
Mr Rao only gives homework to students who sit alone
Arjun should not ask any questions

questions.question: The last line says the last bench 'was not quite as far from everything as it had looked'. It most likely means that:
questions.solution: The distance in the line is emotional, not physical: after meeting Imran, Arjun no longer feels cut off from everyone.
options: Arjun now feels less isolated than he did that morning
the last bench is closer to the board than the others
Arjun has decided to leave the school
Imran will move to another seat

questions.question: The main idea of the passage is that:
questions.solution: The author gives reasons for keeping handwriting and ends by recommending that we keep both tools.
options: handwriting still has value and should be kept alongside typing

questions.question: According to the passage, why might handwritten notes lead to better understanding?
questions.solution: The second paragraph says the writer 'cannot copy everything and must decide what matters', whereas a typist can record almost every word.
options: Handwriting is slow, so the writer must decide what matters
Handwriting is easier to read later

questions.question: The comparison with 'lighting a lamp with a match' suggests that some people see handwriting as:
questions.solution: The author uses the match to show what people mean when they say the skill's 'time has passed'.
options: a skill that has become outdated

questions.question: The author's conclusion is that we should:
questions.solution: The last sentence recommends keeping both: 'the pen when we want to think and the keyboard when we want to produce'.
options: use the pen to think and the keyboard to produce

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT supported by the passage?
questions.solution: The author says that none of this is an argument against keyboards and calls them indispensable for long documents. The claim that typing is 'always worse' is never made.
options: Typing is always worse than handwriting
Keyboards are indispensable for long documents
A signature is still trusted as proof of presence
Some studies link handwritten notes with better understanding

questions.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to PRUDENT.
questions.solution: Prudent means acting with care and good judgement, i.e. cautious. Reckless is its antonym.

questions.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to CONCEAL.
questions.solution: To conceal is to keep something from being seen or known, i.e. to hide. Reveal is its antonym.

questions.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to SCARCE.
questions.solution: Scarce means in short supply, i.e. rare or hard to find. Plentiful is its antonym.

questions.question: Choose the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to GENEROUS.
questions.solution: Generous means willing to give freely; miserly means unwilling to spend or give. Kind is close to the original meaning, not opposite.

questions.question: Choose the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to VICTORY.
questions.solution: Victory is winning; defeat is losing. Triumph and success are synonyms of victory.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: She is allergic ______ peanuts.
questions.solution: The correct preposition after 'allergic' is 'to'.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: I have lived in this town ______ 2015.
questions.solution: 'Since' is used with a point in time (2015). 'For' would be used with a period, such as 'for nine years'.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: Each of the players ______ a medal at the ceremony.
questions.solution: 'Each' takes a singular verb, so 'have received', 'were receiving' and 'are given' (all plural) are wrong. 'Received' works as a past-tense verb with a singular subject.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: Neither of the two answers ______ correct.
questions.solution: 'Neither' is treated as singular, so the singular verb 'is' is required.

questions.question: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) The news about the floods / (B) were broadcast / (C) on every channel / (D) last night.
questions.solution: 'News' is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb. It should be 'was broadcast'. The error is in part B.

questions.question: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) She said me / (B) that she would / (C) come to the party / (D) tomorrow.
questions.solution: 'Said' cannot take a direct person object. It should be 'told me' (or 'said to me'). The error is in part A.

questions.question:
Rearrange the parts to form a meaningful sentence:
P: the scientists   Q: a new species   R: discovered   S: in the deep sea
questions.solution: 'The scientists (P) discovered (R) a new species (Q) in the deep sea (S).' The subject comes first, then the verb, then its object, then the place.

questions.question: Choose the one word that can replace the phrase: a person who can speak many languages.
questions.solution: A polyglot knows and can use several languages. A pedant is overly concerned with detail, a philanthropist helps others with money, and a pessimist expects the worst.

questions.question: Choose the one word that can replace the phrase: a large cage or building in which birds are kept.
questions.solution: An aviary is a place for keeping birds. An apiary is for bees, an aquarium is for fish and an armoury is for weapons.

questions.question:
Match each word in List I with its meaning in List II.
List I: (a) Candid (b) Frugal (c) Lethargic (d) Obstinate
List II: (i) careful not to waste money (ii) stubbornly refusing to change (iii) sluggish and without energy (iv) frank and honest
questions.solution: Candid = frank and honest (iv); Frugal = careful not to waste money (i); Lethargic = sluggish and without energy (iii); Obstinate = stubbornly refusing to change (ii). These are the standard dictionary senses of the four words.

questions.question:
Match each phrase in List I with its meaning in List II.
List I: (a) A blessing in disguise (b) To burn the midnight oil (c) To beat about the bush (d) A red-letter day
List II: (i) to work or study late into the night (ii) a memorable, happy day (iii) to avoid coming to the point (iv) something good that first seemed bad
questions.solution: A blessing in disguise = something good that first seemed bad (iv); To burn the midnight oil = to work or study late into the night (i); To beat about the bush = to avoid coming to the point (iii); A red-letter day = a memorable, happy day (ii). These are the accepted meanings of the four idioms.

questions.question:
Match each word in List I with its antonym in List II.
List I: (a) Transparent (b) Ancient (c) Expand (d) Humble
List II: (i) modern (ii) arrogant (iii) contract (iv) opaque
questions.solution: Transparent = opaque (iv); Ancient = modern (i); Expand = contract (iii); Humble = arrogant (ii). Each pair is a standard pair of opposites.

questions.question:
Match each literary device in List I with its example in List II.
List I: (a) Simile (b) Metaphor (c) Personification (d) Alliteration
List II: (i) Time is a thief. (ii) Peter picked a peck of pickled peppers. (iii) The wind whispered through the trees. (iv) Her smile was like sunshine.
questions.solution: Simile = Her smile was like sunshine. (iv); Metaphor = Time is a thief. (i); Personification = The wind whispered through the trees. (iii); Alliteration = Peter picked a peck of pickled peppers. (ii). A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'; a metaphor states that one thing is another; personification gives human actions to a non-human thing; alliteration repeats the opening consonant sound.

questions.question:
Match each word in List I with its meaning in List II.
List I: (a) Ubiquitous (b) Pragmatic (c) Ambivalent (d) Laconic
List II: (i) dealing with things in a practical way (ii) using very few words (iii) having mixed feelings (iv) found everywhere
questions.solution: Ubiquitous = found everywhere (iv); Pragmatic = dealing with things in a practical way (i); Ambivalent = having mixed feelings (iii); Laconic = using very few words (ii). These are the standard dictionary senses of the four words.

questions.question: Choose the one word that can replace the phrase: a person who does not believe in the existence of God.
questions.solution: An atheist denies that God exists. An agnostic holds that it cannot be known, a heretic rejects the accepted teaching of a religion, and a pagan follows a non-mainstream or older faith.

questions.question: Choose the one word that can replace the phrase: a speech made by a character alone on the stage, speaking their thoughts aloud.
questions.solution: A soliloquy is spoken alone, voicing one's thoughts. A dialogue needs two or more speakers, an epilogue is a closing section, and a monograph is a detailed written study.

questions.question: Choose the one word that can replace the phrase: a government by a small group of powerful people.
questions.solution: Oligarchy is rule by a few. Monarchy is rule by one sovereign, democracy is rule by the people, and anarchy is the absence of government.

questions.question: Choose the one word that can replace the phrase: a word or phrase that reads the same backwards as forwards.
questions.solution: 'Level' and 'madam' are palindromes. An anagram rearranges letters, an acronym is formed from initial letters, and a homonym shares spelling or sound with a different word.

questions.question: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) Although she is / (B) senior than me / (C) by three years, / (D) we joined the firm together.
questions.solution: Adjectives such as senior, junior, superior and inferior take 'to', not 'than'. The correct phrase is 'senior to me', so the error is in part B.

questions.question:
Rearrange the parts to form a meaningful sentence:
P: before sunrise   Q: my grandfather   R: every morning   S: goes for a walk
questions.solution: 'My grandfather (Q) goes for a walk (S) every morning (R) before sunrise (P).' Subject, verb phrase, then how often, then when.

questions.question:
Rearrange the parts to form a meaningful sentence:
P: although it was raining heavily   Q: reached the station   R: on time   S: the students
questions.solution: 'Although it was raining heavily (P), the students (S) reached the station (Q) on time (R).' The concessive clause comes first; the main clause has its subject before the verb and object.

questions.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to CORROBORATE.
questions.solution: To corroborate is to confirm or support a statement with further evidence (a witness corroborates an alibi). 'Collaborate' (work together) and 'corrode' (wear away) only look similar; 'contradict' is nearly the opposite.

questions.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to SPURIOUS.
questions.solution: Spurious means false or not what it claims to be (a spurious claim, a spurious coin). 'Genuine' is its opposite; 'spirited' and 'curious' are sound-alike traps.

questions.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to AUSTERE.
questions.solution: Austere means severe or strict in manner, and plain and without luxury in style (an austere room, an austere life). 'Highly decorated' is the opposite sense; the other two are unrelated.

questions.question: Choose the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to ZENITH.
questions.solution: The zenith is the highest point; the nadir is the lowest point. 'Summit' and 'climax' are near-synonyms of zenith, and the horizon is not an extreme at all.

questions.question: Choose the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to LOQUACIOUS.
questions.solution: Loquacious means very talkative. 'Garrulous' and 'voluble' are synonyms of it, and 'eloquent' (fluent and persuasive) is also about speaking well. Taciturn, meaning saying very little, is the opposite.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: My teacher's ______ helped me choose the right subjects.
questions.solution: A noun is needed after the possessive 'teacher's'. 'Advice' is the noun and is uncountable, so 'advices' is wrong; 'advise' is the verb and 'advised' is its past form.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: The new timetable will ______ every student who joined after April.
questions.solution: 'Affect' is the verb meaning 'to have an influence on'. 'Effect' is normally a noun (as a verb it means 'to bring about', which does not fit), 'infect' refers to disease, and 'afflict' means to cause suffering.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: Hardly had we reached the platform ______ the train began to move.
questions.solution: 'Hardly' and 'scarcely' pair with 'when' (or 'before'): 'Hardly had we reached … when …'. 'Than' belongs with 'no sooner'; 'then' and 'that' do not complete the construction.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: The firm has lost money for three years running; ______, it has decided to close two branches.
questions.solution: Closing branches is a result of the losses, so a connector of result is needed: 'consequently'. 'Nevertheless' signals contrast, 'meanwhile' signals simultaneous time, and 'otherwise' signals an alternative.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: One of my cousins ______ in Chennai.
questions.solution: The subject is 'one' (not 'cousins'), which is singular, so the verb must be singular: 'lives'. The other three are plural forms.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: After the quarrel, the two brothers stopped speaking to ______.
questions.solution: A reciprocal pronoun is needed (each brother stopped speaking to the other): 'each other'. 'Themselves' would mean each spoke to himself, 'ourselves' does not match the subject, and 'one other' is not a reciprocal pronoun.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: If it ______ tomorrow, the match will be postponed.
questions.solution: In a first conditional the if-clause takes the simple present and the main clause takes 'will': 'If it rains tomorrow, the match will be postponed.' 'Will rain' is not used in the if-clause, and 'rained/would rain' belong to the second conditional.

questions.question: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) The furniture / (B) in these rooms / (C) are very old / (D) and needs polishing.
questions.solution: 'Furniture' is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb, as part D already shows ('needs'). So 'are' in part C must be 'is'. Corrected: 'The furniture in these rooms is very old and needs polishing.'

questions.question: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) He is one of those people / (B) who always tries / (C) to help / (D) others in need.
questions.solution: The relative pronoun 'who' refers to 'those people' (plural), not to 'one', so its verb must be plural: 'who always try'. The error is in part B. Corrected: 'He is one of those people who always try to help others in need.'

questions.question: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) No sooner did the bell ring / (B) when the children / (C) rushed out / (D) of the classroom.
questions.solution: 'No sooner' is always followed by 'than', not 'when'. The error is in part B. Corrected: 'No sooner did the bell ring than the children rushed out of the classroom.'

questions.question: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) I prefer reading novels / (B) than watching / (C) films on / (D) my phone.
questions.solution: 'Prefer' takes 'to' for the second item: 'prefer reading novels to watching films'. The error is in part B. Corrected: 'I prefer reading novels to watching films on my phone.'

questions.question: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) Ten kilometres / (B) are a long distance / (C) to walk / (D) in this heat.
questions.solution: A plural amount treated as a single quantity (a distance, a sum of money, a period of time) takes a singular verb: 'Ten kilometres is a long distance'. The error is in part B. Corrected: 'Ten kilometres is a long distance to walk in this heat.'

questions.question: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) Scarcely had I / (B) opened the door / (C) than the cat / (D) ran inside.
questions.solution: 'Scarcely' (like 'hardly') pairs with 'when' or 'before', not 'than'. The error is in part C. Corrected: 'Scarcely had I opened the door when the cat ran inside.'

questions.question: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) The police has / (B) arrested the man / (C) who stole / (D) the bicycle.
questions.solution: 'Police' is a plural noun in English and takes a plural verb: 'The police have arrested …'. The error is in part A. Corrected: 'The police have arrested the man who stole the bicycle.'

questions.question: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: (A) Unless you do not / (B) work hard, / (C) you will not / (D) pass the examination.
questions.solution: 'Unless' already means 'if not', so adding 'do not' creates a double negative. It should be 'Unless you work hard, you will not pass'. The error is in part A. Corrected: 'Unless you work hard, you will not pass the examination.'

questions.question:
Rearrange the parts to form a meaningful sentence:
P: the importance of saving water   Q: the village council   R: through street plays   S: explained to the residents
questions.solution: 'The village council (Q) explained to the residents (S) the importance of saving water (P) through street plays (R).' Subject, verb with its indirect object, the thing explained, then the means.

questions.question:
Rearrange the parts to form a meaningful sentence:
P: was postponed   Q: because of the heavy rain   R: the cricket match   S: scheduled for Sunday
questions.solution: 'The cricket match (R) scheduled for Sunday (S) was postponed (P) because of the heavy rain (Q).' The phrase 'scheduled for Sunday' must follow the noun it describes.

questions.question:
The sentence begins: 'Only…'. Rearrange the parts to complete it:
P: did he realise   Q: after he had left the house   R: his phone   S: that he had forgotten
questions.solution: 'Only after he had left the house (Q) did he realise (P) that he had forgotten (S) his phone (R).' A sentence opening with 'Only after …' requires inversion in the main clause ('did he realise'), which must come directly after the time clause.

questions.question:
Rearrange the parts to form a meaningful sentence:
P: a balanced diet   Q: doctors recommend   R: and regular exercise   S: for a healthy life
questions.solution: 'Doctors recommend (Q) a balanced diet (P) and regular exercise (R) for a healthy life (S).' 'And regular exercise' must follow the first item it is joined to.

questions.question:
Rearrange the parts to form a meaningful sentence:
P: who had been missing for two days   Q: the police found   R: the little boy   S: in a nearby forest
questions.solution: 'The police found (Q) the little boy (R) who had been missing for two days (P) in a nearby forest (S).' The relative clause must come right after 'the little boy', the person it describes.

questions.question:
Rearrange the parts to form a meaningful sentence:
P: but also writes her own songs   Q: not only sings   R: the young artist   S: beautifully
questions.solution: 'The young artist (R) not only sings (Q) beautifully (S) but also writes her own songs (P).' 'Not only' must come before 'but also', and the adverb 'beautifully' belongs with 'sings'.

questions.question:
Rearrange the parts to form a meaningful sentence:
P: than any other student   Q: worked harder   R: in the class   S: Priya
questions.solution: 'Priya (S) worked harder (Q) than any other student (P) in the class (R).' The comparison 'than any other student' is completed by 'in the class'.

questions.question:
Rearrange the parts to form a meaningful sentence:
P: the bridge   Q: built over a century ago   R: still carries   S: heavy traffic every day
questions.solution: 'The bridge (P) built over a century ago (Q) still carries (R) heavy traffic every day (S).' The participle phrase describes the bridge and is followed by the verb and its object.

questions.question:
Match each word in List I with its meaning in List II.
List I: (a) Verbose (b) Ominous (c) Resilient (d) Tenacious
List II: (i) suggesting that something bad will happen (ii) holding firmly to a purpose (iii) able to recover quickly from difficulty (iv) using more words than needed
questions.solution: Verbose = using more words than needed (iv); Ominous = suggesting that something bad will happen (i); Resilient = able to recover quickly from difficulty (iii); Tenacious = holding firmly to a purpose (ii). These are the standard dictionary senses of the four words.

questions.question:
Match each idiom in List I with its meaning in List II.
List I: (a) A piece of cake (b) Once in a blue moon (c) To spill the beans (d) To hit the sack
List II: (i) very rarely (ii) to go to bed (iii) to reveal a secret (iv) something very easy
questions.solution: A piece of cake = something very easy (iv); Once in a blue moon = very rarely (i); To spill the beans = to reveal a secret (iii); To hit the sack = to go to bed (ii). These are the accepted meanings of the four idioms.

questions.question:
Match each collective phrase in List I with the noun it is used for in List II.
List I: (a) A pride of (b) A swarm of (c) A school of (d) A herd of
List II: (i) bees (ii) cattle (iii) fish (iv) lions
questions.solution: A pride of = lions (iv); A swarm of = bees (i); A school of = fish (iii); A herd of = cattle (ii). A pride of lions, a swarm of bees, a school of fish and a herd of cattle are the standard collective expressions.

questions.question:
Match each word in List I with its antonym in List II.
List I: (a) Optimist (b) Benign (c) Lenient (d) Affluent
List II: (i) malignant (ii) impoverished (iii) strict (iv) pessimist
questions.solution: Optimist = pessimist (iv); Benign = malignant (i); Lenient = strict (iii); Affluent = impoverished (ii). Each pair is a standard pair of opposites: hopeful/gloomy, harmless/harmful, mild/severe in discipline, and rich/poor.

questions.question:
Match each figure of speech in List I with its example in List II.
List I: (a) Oxymoron (b) Onomatopoeia (c) Hyperbole (d) Irony
List II: (i) the buzz of the bees (ii) The fire station burned down. (iii) I have told you a million times. (iv) a deafening silence
questions.solution: Oxymoron = a deafening silence (iv); Onomatopoeia = the buzz of the bees (i); Hyperbole = I have told you a million times. (iii); Irony = The fire station burned down. (ii). An oxymoron joins contradictory words; onomatopoeia imitates a sound; hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration; irony (here, situational) is an outcome opposite to what one would expect.

questions.question:
Match each phrasal verb in List I with its meaning in List II.
List I: (a) Put off (b) Give up (c) Look after (d) Turn down
List II: (i) stop trying (ii) reject (iii) take care of (iv) postpone
questions.solution: Put off = postpone (iv); Give up = stop trying (i); Look after = take care of (iii); Turn down = reject (ii). These are the common meanings of the four phrasal verbs.

questions.question:
Match each specialist in List I with what he or she studies or collects in List II.
List I: (a) Ornithologist (b) Entomologist (c) Seismologist (d) Numismatist
List II: (i) insects (ii) coins (iii) earthquakes (iv) birds
questions.solution: Ornithologist = birds (iv); Entomologist = insects (i); Seismologist = earthquakes (iii); Numismatist = coins (ii). Ornith- (bird), entomo- (insect), seismo- (shaking) and numism- (coin) give the four meanings. Entomologist is often confused with etymologist, who studies word origins.

questions.question: Choose the one word that can replace the phrase: a person who walks in his or her sleep.
questions.solution: Somnambulist (Latin somnus 'sleep' + ambulare 'to walk') is a sleepwalker. An insomniac cannot sleep, a pedestrian walks on the road, and a hypochondriac worries excessively about illness.

questions.question: Choose the one word that can replace the phrase: a remedy for all diseases or problems.
questions.solution: A panacea is a cure-all. A placebo is a dummy treatment, an antidote counters one particular poison, and a vaccine protects against one particular disease.

questions.question: Choose the one word that can replace the phrase: an extreme fear of heights.
questions.solution: Acro- means height or top. Claustrophobia is fear of enclosed spaces, hydrophobia of water, and agoraphobia of open or crowded public places.

questions.question: Choose the one word that can replace the phrase: handwriting that cannot be read.
questions.solution: Illegible means not readable. Ineligible means not qualified, indelible means impossible to erase, and inaudible means impossible to hear.

questions.question: Choose the one word that can replace the phrase: a person who eats far too much.
questions.solution: A glutton eats excessively. A gourmet is a connoisseur of fine food, a carnivore eats meat, and a cannibal eats the flesh of its own kind.

questions.question: Choose the one word that can replace the phrase: a list of items to be discussed at a meeting.
questions.solution: The agenda is the list drawn up before a meeting; the minutes record what was said afterwards. An itinerary is a travel plan and a memorandum is a written note or message.

questions.question: Choose the one word that can replace the phrase: a person who endures pain or hardship without showing feelings or complaining.
questions.solution: A stoic bears hardship calmly. A cynic distrusts people's motives, a sceptic doubts claims, and a hedonist pursues pleasure, which is nearly the opposite.

questions.question: Choose the one word that can replace the phrase: words written on a tombstone in memory of the person buried there.
questions.solution: An epitaph is the inscription on a tomb. An epigram is a short witty saying, an epilogue is a closing section of a book or play, and an epithet is a descriptive name such as 'Alexander the Great'.

questions.question: According to the passage, the boundary that marks the end of one year's growth lies between:
questions.solution: Paragraph 1: 'The sharp boundary between one summer's dark wood and the next spring's pale wood marks the edge of a year.' Ring width (wide or narrow) is about weather, not the year boundary, and the bark is not discussed.
options: a wide ring and a narrow ring
two pale rings formed in the same spring
the bark and the outermost ring
the small, dark late-summer wood and the next spring's wide, pale wood

questions.question: A tree shows an unusually narrow ring for a particular year. By the passage's account, that year was most probably:
questions.solution: Paragraph 2: 'In a wet, mild year a tree lays down a broad ring; in a year of drought, a narrow one.' So a narrow ring points to drought. Planting or cutting is not linked to ring width.
options: the year the tree was planted
a year in which the tree was cut

questions.question: The comparison with 'people in one town' who 'share memories of the same hard winters' is used to explain why:
questions.solution: The simile follows 'every tree in a region feels the same weather', so trees there 'share the same pattern', just as townspeople share memories of the same winters. It is an analogy for a common record, not a claim about memory, building or estimating age.
options: old trees remember past weather better than young ones
trees of one species in a region show the same pattern of wide and narrow rings
towns were often built from local timber
people can estimate a tree's age by looking at it

questions.question: Records 'thousands of years long' are possible mainly because:
questions.solution: Paragraph 3 says the shared pattern lets scientists 'reach far beyond the life of any single tree' by matching a living tree with an old beam, and that beam with older timber. The passage does not rely on very old living trees; rainfall records are said not to go back that far ('long before anyone measured rainfall'); and paintings and ships are things dated by the method, not sources for it.
options: the ring patterns of overlapping pieces of wood of different ages can be matched and linked
some living trees are thousands of years old
rainfall has been measured for thousands of years
paintings and ships record the dates on which they were made

questions.question: What assumption about placebos do the trials described in the passage challenge?
questions.solution: Paragraph 1 states the old assumption: a placebo 'could work only if the patient was deceived'. Paragraph 2 says the trials 'challenged this assumption' by telling patients exactly what they were taking. The other options are not under challenge.
options: That a placebo contains no active ingredient
That a placebo can work only if the patient is deceived
That back pain is a long-lasting condition
That sugar pills are cheap to produce

questions.question: According to the researchers, honest placebos may work because:
questions.solution: Paragraph 2: 'the ritual of treatment, the act of taking something regularly with care and attention, may itself prompt the body and mind to respond.' The passage gives no support for secret belief, an effect of sugar, or selective prescribing.
options: patients secretly believe the pills contain medicine
the ritual of taking a treatment with care and attention may itself prompt a response
sugar has a mild pain-relieving effect
doctors give the pills only to patients who are already recovering

questions.question: The author mentions that the conditions studied are 'ones in which patients themselves report how they feel' in order to:
questions.solution: The remark is part of the author's 'caution', and is followed by the contrast between a headache feeling less severe and shrinking a tumour. The point is a limit on what has been shown, not an accusation of lying. 'Should replace pain medicines' contradicts 'not a substitute', and the trials are called small, not large.
options: argue that honest placebos should replace pain medicines
prove that the patients in the trials were not telling the truth
suggest that the benefits found may be limited to how symptoms are felt, not to measurable disease
show that the trials were too large to be reliable

questions.question: Which statement best expresses the author's conclusion?
questions.solution: The final paragraph says honest placebos 'are not a substitute for medicine' but may show that the way care is given 'can be part of' treatment. 'As effective as most medicines' and 'cure any illness' overstate the evidence, and the passage praises honest placebos for removing the ethical problem rather than calling them unethical.
options: Honest placebos are as effective as most medicines
The way care is given can be part of a treatment, though honest placebos cannot replace real medicine
Placebos are unethical and should not be used
The trials prove that the mind can cure any illness

questions.question: Why was this Joseph's last evening at the lighthouse?
questions.solution: The department's letter says the light 'would be made automatic in March' with a machine switching it on and off and a technician visiting twice a year. Nothing suggests dismissal, a request from the granddaughter, or closure of the light.
options: His granddaughter had asked him to stop working
He had been dismissed after an inspector's visit
The light was being made automatic, so a keeper was no longer needed
The lighthouse was being closed to shipping

questions.question: The detail that Joseph knew 'each step by its sound' mainly suggests:
questions.solution: After thirty-one years of nightly climbs he knows the seventh step rings and the fortieth is cracked; the detail conveys intimate familiarity. The passage gives no hint of danger, poor eyesight or dislike.
options: that the staircase was dangerous and needed repair
how long and closely he had lived with the lighthouse
that he disliked climbing the steps

questions.question: Joseph's reply, 'The machine knows when it is dark. That is most of the job,' most likely reveals:
questions.solution: He pauses ('considered this'), concedes that the machine covers 'most' of the job, and so implies a remainder (attention to the boats) it cannot cover. The tone is restrained, not angry, and he neither praises the machine as better nor tries to frighten the girl.
options: a quiet acceptance mixed with the sense that something the machine cannot do is being lost
his belief that the machine will do the work better than he did
anger at the department for replacing him
that he wants to frighten his granddaughter about the boats

questions.question: How does Joseph respond to the department's letter?
questions.solution: 'Joseph read it twice, folded it into a careful square and put it under the clock.' The careful, silent handling shows restraint. There is no tearing, protest letter or immediate telling.
options: With restraint: he reads it twice, folds it carefully and puts it away
With open anger, tearing it up
By writing a letter of protest
By telling his granddaughter about it at once

cu-handwriting.title: Discursive passage: In defence of handwriting
cu-handwriting.html:
Discursive passage: In defence of handwriting

Few people write by hand for long these days. Messages are typed, notes are dictated and even shopping lists live on phones. It is easy to say that handwriting is a skill whose time has passed, like lighting a lamp with a match. But before we let it go, we might ask what it quietly does for us.

Several small studies suggest that students who take notes by hand tend to understand lecture material a little better than those who type. The explanation offered is simple: handwriting is slow, so the writer cannot copy everything and must decide what matters. Typing is fast enough to record almost every word, and the typist may leave the lecture with pages of text and little thought behind them.

Handwriting also carries something of the writer. A letter in a familiar hand can comfort a reader in a way that a printed page cannot, and a signature is still trusted as proof of a person's presence.

None of this is an argument against keyboards, which are faster, tidier and indispensable for long documents. It is only an argument against giving up one tool simply because another has arrived. The sensible course is to keep both, using the pen when we want to think and the keyboard when we want to produce.

cu-lastbench.title: Narrative passage: The last bench
cu-lastbench.html:
Narrative passage: The last bench

Arjun's family had moved cities in the middle of the school year, and on his first morning he walked into Class IX with his bag held tightly in front of him, as if it were a shield. The teacher pointed to the only empty seat, on the last bench by the window. He sat down and looked at the board without really reading it.

At the break, the others drifted out in noisy groups. Arjun stayed, pretending to search his bag. He knew nobody here, and he had decided, quite firmly, that it was easier not to try.

"You can have the window seat," said a voice. A boy with a patched blue bag had stopped beside the bench. "I always sit here, but nobody comes this far back anyway." He laughed, as though it were a joke against himself. "I'm Imran. We have maths next. Mr Rao gives homework before he even says good morning."

Arjun almost smiled. "Is it hard?"

"Only if you're alone," said Imran, and pulled out a spare notebook. "Copy the last class's notes from mine. I'll show you which ones matter."

By the end of the day Arjun had stopped holding his bag like a shield. He did not know yet whether he would like the city or the school. But the last bench, he thought, was not quite as far from everything as it had looked that morning.

cu-lighthouse.title: Literary passage: The last keeper
cu-lighthouse.html:
Literary passage: The last keeper

For thirty-one years Joseph Fernandes had climbed the hundred and twelve steps of the lighthouse every evening at dusk. He knew each step by its sound: the seventh rang slightly, the fortieth had a crack his boot always found, and the last ten groaned like an old man rising from a chair. At the top he would wipe the great lens, light the lamp and write the time in a ledger that nobody but the inspector ever read.

The letter from the department was polite. The light would be made automatic in March; a small machine would switch it on and off by itself, and a technician would visit twice a year. His service, it said, had been "much appreciated". Joseph read it twice, folded it into a careful square and put it under the clock.

On his last evening his granddaughter came with him. She counted the steps aloud and complained halfway up. At the top she pressed her face to the glass and watched the beam sweep out across the dark water, catching for an instant the white edge of a fishing boat.

"Does the machine know about the boats?" she asked.

Joseph considered this. "The machine knows when it is dark," he said at last. "That is most of the job."

He wrote the time in the ledger, and then, after a moment, he wrote something else beneath it, which he did not let her read.

cu-mangrove.title: Factual passage: Mangroves
cu-mangrove.html:
Factual passage: Mangroves

Along many tropical coasts, where rivers meet the sea, grow forests that seem to stand on stilts. These are mangroves, trees and shrubs that can survive in salty, waterlogged mud that would kill most other plants. Some mangroves filter much of the salt out at their roots; others get rid of it through their leaves. Because the mud holds very little oxygen, several species send up pencil-like roots from the ground. These breathing roots, called pneumatophores, take in air at low tide.

Mangroves matter far beyond the narrow strip they occupy. Their tangled roots slow down waves and trap sediment, so they help protect the shore from erosion and reduce the damage done by storm surges. The calm, shaded water between the roots is a nursery for young fish, crabs and prawns, many of which later move out to the open sea, where they support coastal fishing. Mangrove soils also store large amounts of carbon that would otherwise add to the carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

Despite these benefits, mangroves have been cleared in many places for fish farms, ports and housing. Once removed, they are slow to return, because seedlings need sheltered mud and the right mix of fresh and salt water to take root. Restoration projects tend to succeed when local communities, who depend on the forest for fish and firewood, are involved in planting and protecting it. Without such involvement, newly planted areas are often lost again within a few years.

cu-monsoon.title: Literary passage: The first rain
cu-monsoon.html:
Literary passage: The first rain

The first rain of the monsoon does not arrive so much as announce itself. For days the sky has been a sheet of tin, the air thick enough to lean on, and the city has waited with the irritable patience of a queue that has stopped moving. Then the wind changes. Leaves turn their pale undersides to the sky, as if to check what is coming, and somewhere a door bangs shut.

When the drops come, they are large and few, each one landing on the dusty road with a sound like a coin dropped on a table. Children run out before their mothers can stop them. Shopkeepers, who have spent the week complaining of the heat, stand in their doorways and complain instead about the mud, though their faces say otherwise.

And then there is the smell. The parched earth, touched by water, releases a scent so particular that we have borrowed a scientist's word, petrichor, to name it, though no word quite contains it. For a moment the whole city seems to breathe out.

By evening the gutters are rivers and the traffic has given up. Tomorrow there will be potholes, leaking roofs and the long grey weeks of the season. But tonight nobody is thinking of tomorrow. Tonight the rain is not weather; it is a reprieve.

cu-placebo.title: Discursive passage: The honest placebo
cu-placebo.html:
Discursive passage: The honest placebo

A placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill. For decades doctors assumed that it could work only if the patient was deceived. If you knew the pill was sugar, the reasoning went, your expectation of relief would vanish, and with it any benefit.

A series of small trials has challenged this assumption. Patients with certain long-lasting conditions, such as some kinds of back pain, were handed bottles plainly labelled as placebo and told exactly what was inside. Many nevertheless reported less discomfort than patients who received no pills at all. The researchers suggest that the ritual of treatment, the act of taking something regularly with care and attention, may itself prompt the body and mind to respond.

The finding is attractive because it seems to remove an ethical problem. Giving fake medicine without telling the patient is a kind of lying; an honest placebo involves no lie at all. Yet caution is needed. The trials have mostly been short and small, and the conditions studied are ones in which patients themselves report how they feel. A sugar pill may make a headache feel less severe; there is no good evidence that it can shrink a tumour or cure an infection.

The lesson, then, is narrower than the headlines suggest. Honest placebos are not a substitute for medicine. What they may show is that the way care is given, including the time and attention a patient receives, is not merely decoration around a treatment but can be part of it.

cu-radio.title: Narrative passage: The radio
cu-radio.html:
Narrative passage: The radio

The radio had been silent for eleven years when Meera carried it down from the loft. It was a heavy wooden box with a cracked dial and a smell of dust and old varnish. Her grandfather watched from his chair as she set it on the table.

"It won't work," he said. "Nothing in it has worked since your grandmother passed away."

Meera said nothing. She had spent the summer helping at her uncle's repair shop, and she had learned that most broken things were not as broken as people believed. She unscrewed the back panel. Inside, among the glass valves and coloured wires, she found what she had half expected: a wire that had come loose from its terminal, its end green with corrosion.

It took her most of the afternoon. She cleaned the terminal, cut back the wire and borrowed her uncle's soldering iron. Her grandfather pretended to read the newspaper, but she noticed that he had not turned a page in an hour.

When she finally switched it on, there was only a low hum. Then, slowly, as the valves warmed, a voice rose out of the static, reading the evening news in the same calm tone the old man must have heard a thousand times.

He put down the newspaper. For a long moment he did not speak. Then he reached over and turned the dial, very carefully, to a station that played old film songs.

"She liked this one," he said quietly, and Meera understood that she had repaired more than a radio.

cu-sleep.title: Factual passage: Sleep and learning
cu-sleep.html:
Factual passage: Sleep and learning

Most students know the feeling of studying late into the night and then struggling to remember anything the next day. Research on sleep suggests that this is not just bad luck. During sleep, the brain appears to replay and strengthen what was learned during the day, helping to move new information into long-term memory. A student who sleeps well after studying may therefore recall more than one who stays awake revising for the same extra hours.

Sleep matters for another reason: attention. A tired mind finds it harder to focus, makes more careless mistakes and is slower to solve problems. These effects are small after one bad night but add up when short sleep becomes a habit.

Teenagers face a particular difficulty. During adolescence the body's internal clock tends to shift later, so many teenagers do not feel sleepy until late at night, yet school often begins early in the morning. Some schools that moved their start times later have reported better attendance and alertness, though researchers caution that results vary and that more studies are needed.

None of this means that studying late is always a mistake; an occasional late night before an exam may be unavoidable. But the evidence suggests that sleep is part of studying, not a break from it. A regular bedtime, a dark room and keeping phones away from the bed are simple steps that cost nothing and may help.

cu-stepwell.title: Factual passage: Stepwells
cu-stepwell.html:
Factual passage: Stepwells

In the dry parts of western India, people once solved the problem of water not by building walls around it but by digging down to meet it. The result was the stepwell, known as a vav or baoli: a well so wide that a flight of steps could lead from the ground to the water below. As the water level rose and fell with the seasons, villagers simply walked down or up to reach it.

Stepwells were more than water tanks. The cool, shaded air at the bottom made them places to rest in the heat of the day, and travellers on long trade routes often stopped at them. Many were decorated with carved pillars, balconies and sculpted figures, because the people who paid for them saw the gift of water as an act of merit. Some, like Rani ki Vav in Gujarat, are now World Heritage sites.

Their decline began when piped water and hand pumps arrived. Once water could be drawn without walking down a hundred steps, many stepwells were abandoned, filled with rubbish or used as dumps. Yet some are being given new life. Volunteers have cleared silt, repaired walls and let rainwater flow back in. The lesson, they say, is practical as well as historical: structures that store rain where it falls may be useful again in regions where groundwater is running low.

cu-treerings.title: Factual passage: Reading the rings of trees
cu-treerings.html:
Factual passage: Reading the rings of trees

Cut across the trunk of an old oak and you will see a series of rings, one for each year of the tree's life. In spring a tree grows quickly and makes wide, pale cells; by late summer growth slows and the cells become small and dark. The sharp boundary between one summer's dark wood and the next spring's pale wood marks the edge of a year.

Counting rings gives a tree's age, but their real value lies in their widths. In a wet, mild year a tree lays down a broad ring; in a year of drought, a narrow one. Because every tree in a region feels the same weather, trees of the same species there share the same pattern of wide and narrow rings, much as people in one town share memories of the same hard winters.

This shared pattern lets scientists reach far beyond the life of any single tree. The inner rings of a living tree can be matched with the outer rings of a beam from an old building, whose inner rings can then be matched with timber older still. Linked in this way, overlapping pieces of wood have produced continuous records thousands of years long.

Such records have practical uses. A wooden panel on which a painting was made can be dated, and so can a ship found on the seabed. Ring patterns also preserve a history of past droughts long before anyone measured rainfall, a history that helps planners judge how severe a dry spell might one day become.
